replies: Sam: Hey! For tonight, I'd go with cacio e pepe — it's quick, just pasta, cheese, and black pepper, so you're eating in like twenty minutes. If you've got some garlic and chili flakes, that makes it even better. Want me to put together the steps?
Robin: One thing first — pepper can be a bit rough on a sensitive stomach. Start light with the black pepper and build up as you go; no need for the full shaker unless your tummy agrees.

rows.say: and what wine goes with it
replies: Sam: A crisp white like Vermentino or a dry Pinot Grigio works well — it keeps things light so the cheese and pepper stay front and centre. If you've got a glass of something heavier, save it for another night; this dish is too delicate to get buried under tannins.

rows.say: My dad passed away last week and I have to say a few words at the funeral. I don't know where to start.
replies: Sam: I'm so sorry about your dad. For the words, think of it as three small pieces rather than a speech. First, say his name and how you felt about him, keeping it to one or two lines. Then pick one memory that feels true — a habit, a joke, something he did — and tell it simply. Finally, close with what you want people to carry forward from him, or how you'll keep his spirit close. Write it down first, even if it's just bullet points, so your hands don't have to remember everything. rows.say: Is it safe to leave my dog in the car for ten minutes while I pop into a shop on a warm day?
replies: Sam: No, please don't. Even ten minutes in a warm car can be deadly; temperatures inside a closed vehicle climb fast enough to cause heatstroke quickly. Dogs can't cool themselves like we do, and windows or sunshades won't save them. If you must step away, bring the dog with you—leash on their back if they're small—or keep them in the car only when it's cool and shaded, never on a warm day. From memory · checked
Robin: One quick addition: watch for heavy panting, drooling or collapse — those are heatstroke red flags. If you see any, get to an emergency vet straight away; don't wait to see if it settles.

chime.raw: [{"seat":"steward","point":"Watch for heatstroke signs like heavy panting; seek emergency vet care if seen."}]

rows.say: Robin, is ten minutes really enough to hurt a dog?
replies: Robin: Yeah, ten minutes is genuinely enough to hurt them. In direct sun, a parked car can hit 45°C or more within minutes, even if it’s only warm outside. A dog’s body temperature climbs quickly because they rely on panting and their paws to cool down, which doesn’t work well in a hot, closed space. Even with the windows cracked, it barely slows things down. If you’re ever stuck in that situation, bring them in or get them out immediately—don’t gamble on it. ! Careful: Don't gamble on it; bring them in or get them out immediately if stuck.
